# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutical Analysis I is the first analytical chemistry paper of B.Pharm. It is half theory (principles, indicators, electrodes) and half calculation (molarity, standardisation factors, percentage purity, error statistics). Study one unit a day: read the notes, redo every worked calculation with a calculator without looking, write each reaction and equivalence statement from memory, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 3 is the largest (precipitation, complexometry, gravimetry and diazotisation), so give it two days.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with reactions, equivalence statement and a worked calculation or diagram.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Fundamentals | Primary and secondary standards, preparation and standardisation of titrants, errors (types, minimising), accuracy vs precision, sources of impurities, limit tests (chloride, sulphate, iron, arsenic) |
| 2 Acid–base and non-aqueous | Theories of indicators, neutralisation curves, choice of indicator, non-aqueous solvents, levelling effect, assay of sodium benzoate and ephedrine HCl |
| 3 Precipitation, complexometry, gravimetry, diazotisation | Mohr, Volhard, Fajans methods; EDTA and metal ion indicators; masking and demasking; MgSO4 and calcium gluconate assays; steps of gravimetry, co- and post-precipitation; diazotisation |
| 4 Redox | Iodimetry vs iodometry, cerimetry with advantages, bromatometry, dichrometry, potassium iodate (Andrews) titration, redox indicators |
| 5 Electrochemical | Conductometric titration curves, reference electrodes (SHE, calomel, Ag/AgCl), glass electrode, end-point methods in potentiometry, DME, Ilkovic equation, polarogram |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. For every assay answer write four things: the **reaction**, the **conditions** (medium, pH, temperature), the **indicator with its colour change**, and the **equivalence statement** ("1 ml of 0.1 M … ≡ … g of …"). Examiners look for all four.
2. Calculations: write the formula, substitute with units, show the factor (f = actual ÷ nominal molarity), and box the answer. Method marks are given even when arithmetic slips.
3. Check an equivalence statement yourself: g per ml = Mw × molarity of titrant × (moles of analyte per mole of titrant) ÷ 1000. If your number does not match the molecular weight this way, recheck the stoichiometry.
4. Remember the n factors: KMnO4 5, K2Cr2O7 6, KBrO3 6, Ce⁴⁺ 1, I2 2, thiosulphate 1, oxalic acid 2, H2SO4 2. Normality = molarity × n.
5. Draw the curve that goes with the topic: neutralisation curves with indicator ranges, conductometric V and two-break curves, potentiometric S curve with first and second derivatives, the polarogram with E½ and id, the Gutzeit apparatus, the calomel and glass electrodes, the DME.
6. Use comparison tables for "differentiate" questions: iodimetry vs iodometry, co- vs post-precipitation, accuracy vs precision, determinate vs indeterminate errors, primary vs secondary standards, Mohr vs Volhard.
7. In limit test answers state the principle, the reason for each reagent (nitric acid, citric acid, thioglycollic acid, lead acetate cotton wool, stannous chloride), and how the result is read (sample less than standard = passes).
8. Practise the statistics example (mean, SD, RSD) once a week; it is an easy 5 marks.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics fully: **errors with accuracy, precision and RSD**, **limit tests (chloride, sulphate, iron, arsenic)**, **non-aqueous titrations with solvents and the two assays**, **complexometric titrations with indicators, masking and the two assays**, and **reference and indicator electrodes with potentiometric end points**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Formulas to write without thinking**

| --- | --- | --- |
| M = (w/Mw) × (1000/V ml); N = M × n | Concentration | 1 |
| C1V1 = C2V2 | Dilution | 1 |
| f = actual M ÷ nominal M = expected V ÷ used V | Molarity factor | 1 |
| % = (V − blank) × f × (g per ml) × 100 / w | Assay result | All |
| x̄ = Σx/n; s = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)]; RSD = s/x̄ × 100 | Precision | 1 |

**One-line contrasts examiners like**

| Pair | Difference |
| --- | --- |
| Accuracy vs precision | Closeness to the true value vs closeness of results to each other |
| Determinate vs indeterminate error | Known cause, one direction, correctable vs random, both directions, reduced by averaging |
| Primary vs secondary standard | Weighed to exact strength vs strength found by standardisation |
| Iodimetry vs iodometry | Direct titration with I2 (reductants) vs liberated I2 titrated with thiosulphate (oxidants) |
| Mohr vs Volhard | Direct, neutral, chromate vs back titration, nitric acid, ferric alum |
| Co- vs post-precipitation | During (less on digestion) vs after (more on standing) |
| Protogenic vs protophilic solvent | Acidic, for weak bases (glacial acetic acid) vs basic, for weak acids (DMF, pyridine) |
| Levelling vs differentiating | Makes strengths look equal (water for strong acids) vs shows real differences (glacial acetic acid) |
| Masking vs demasking | Hiding an interfering ion in a complex vs releasing it (formaldehyde frees Zn from cyanide) |
| Reference vs indicator electrode | Constant potential vs potential depends on analyte |
| DME vs RPE | Renewed surface, negative potentials vs rotating Pt, positive potentials, amperometry |

# Limit test for chloride

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for chloride on the given sample as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia and report whether it passes.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow the monograph, your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Chloride ions react with silver nitrate in the presence of dilute nitric acid to form silver chloride, which, at the low levels allowed, stays as a faint white **opalescence** (not a heavy precipitate):

Cl⁻ + AgNO3 → AgCl (white) + NO3⁻

The opalescence of the test solution is compared with that of a **standard** containing a known amount of chloride (the permitted limit), under identical conditions, in matched **Nessler cylinders**. If the test is less opalescent than the standard, the sample passes.

Nitric acid keeps the solution acidic so that carbonate, phosphate and other ions do not precipitate with silver, and it helps form a fine, even opalescence.

## Requirements

Nessler cylinders (50 ml, matched pair), glass rods, pipettes, measuring cylinder; dilute nitric acid, silver nitrate solution (about 5% w/v), chloride standard solution (for example 0.05845% w/v NaCl, of which 1 ml contains 0.355 mg Cl), the sample, distilled water.

## Procedure

**Test**

1. Dissolve the quantity of sample stated in the monograph in water (or prepare the solution as directed) and transfer to a Nessler cylinder.
2. Add 10 ml of dilute nitric acid.
3. Dilute with water to about 50 ml (or to the stated volume, leaving room for the reagent).
4. Add 1 ml of silver nitrate solution, stir immediately with a glass rod and keep aside for 5 minutes, protected from light.

**Standard**

5. In the second cylinder, take the stated volume of chloride standard solution (for example 1 ml of 0.05845% w/v NaCl).
6. Add 10 ml of dilute nitric acid, dilute to the same volume, add 1 ml silver nitrate solution, stir and keep for 5 minutes.

**Comparison**

7. Place both cylinders side by side against a **black background** and view vertically down the length of the cylinders.

## Observations

| Cylinder | Opalescence |
| --- | --- |
| Standard | Faint white opalescence |
| Test | ___ (less / more than standard) |

**Amount in the standard (worked):** 1 ml of 0.05845% w/v NaCl contains 0.5845 mg NaCl; chloride = 0.5845 × 35.45/58.44 = **0.355 mg Cl**. If 1 g of sample is taken, the limit is 0.355 mg per g = 355 ppm.

## Result

The opalescence of the test solution is less / more than that of the standard. The sample **passes / fails** the limit test for chloride.

## Precautions

1. Use matched Nessler cylinders and the same volumes and times for test and standard.
2. Add reagents to both cylinders in the same order and stir in the same way.
3. Avoid direct sunlight (silver chloride darkens).
4. Use chloride-free water and clean glassware.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a limit test?** A semi-quantitative test that shows whether an impurity is below its permitted limit by comparison with a standard.
2. **Why is nitric acid added?** To prevent precipitation of silver carbonate, phosphate and similar salts, and to give a uniform opalescence.
3. **Why not HCl or H2SO4?** HCl adds chloride; sulphuric acid could precipitate silver sulphate at higher concentrations.
4. **Why a black background?** White opalescence is seen best against black.
5. **Why Nessler cylinders?** They are matched in diameter and glass, so equal depths of liquid can be compared fairly.
6. **What if the sample is coloured?** Treat as the monograph directs (for example filter, or use a modified method), since colour hides opalescence.

# Limit test for sulphate

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for sulphate on the given sample as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow the monograph, your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Sulphate ions react with barium chloride in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid to form barium sulphate, which appears as a white **turbidity**:

SO4²⁻ + BaCl2 → BaSO4 (white) + 2Cl⁻

The turbidity of the test is compared with that of a standard containing a known amount of sulphate. **Hydrochloric acid** prevents precipitation of barium carbonate, phosphate and oxalate. The **barium sulphate reagent** (barium chloride solution containing a little sulphate in alcohol) supplies tiny seed crystals of BaSO4 so that the turbidity forms quickly and evenly; alcohol lowers the solubility of BaSO4.

## Requirements

Nessler cylinders (50 ml), glass rods, pipettes; dilute hydrochloric acid, barium sulphate reagent, sulphate standard solution (for example 0.1089% w/v K2SO4, 1 ml of which contains 0.6 mg SO4), sample, distilled water.

## Procedure

**Test**

1. Dissolve the stated quantity of sample in water in a Nessler cylinder.
2. Add 2 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid.
3. Dilute with water to 45 ml.
4. Add 5 ml of barium sulphate reagent, stir immediately and keep for 5 minutes.

**Standard**

5. Take the stated volume of sulphate standard solution (for example 1 ml of 0.1089% w/v K2SO4) in the second cylinder, add 2 ml dilute HCl, dilute to 45 ml, add 5 ml barium sulphate reagent, stir and keep for 5 minutes.

**Comparison**

6. View both cylinders vertically against a **black background** (or as directed) and compare turbidity.

## Observations and calculation

| Cylinder | Turbidity |
| --- | --- |
| Standard | White turbidity |
| Test | ___ |

**Amount in the standard:** 1 ml of 0.1089% w/v K2SO4 = 1.089 mg K2SO4 (Mw 174.26); sulphate = 1.089 × 96.06/174.26 = **0.600 mg SO4**. For a 1 g sample this is a limit of 600 ppm.

## Result

The turbidity of the test is less / more than the standard; the sample **passes / fails** the limit test for sulphate.

## Precautions

1. Treat test and standard identically (volumes, order, time, stirring).
2. Stir immediately after adding the reagent.
3. Use sulphate-free reagents and clean cylinders.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is HCl added?** To stop barium carbonate, phosphate and similar salts from precipitating.
2. **What is the barium sulphate reagent?** Barium chloride solution with alcohol and a trace of potassium sulphate that gives seed crystals.
3. **Why is alcohol present?** It lowers the solubility of BaSO4 and helps uniform turbidity.
4. **Why the seed crystals?** Without them a supersaturated solution may form and turbidity appears slowly and unevenly.
5. **Is a limit test quantitative?** No, semi-quantitative: it only says within or above the limit.

# Limit test for iron

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for iron on the given sample as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow the monograph, your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Iron (as Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺) reacts with **thioglycollic acid** in an ammoniacal solution containing **citric acid** to give a **purple** ferrous thioglycollate complex. The colour of the test is compared with that of a standard containing a known amount of iron.

- Thioglycollic acid reduces any Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and forms the coloured complex, so all iron is detected.
- Citric acid forms a soluble complex with iron and prevents its precipitation as hydroxide when ammonia is added.
- Ammonia makes the solution alkaline; the purple colour develops only in alkaline medium.

## Requirements

Nessler cylinders, pipettes, glass rods; iron-free citric acid solution (20% w/v), thioglycollic acid, iron-free ammonia solution, iron standard solution (prepared from ferric ammonium sulphate), sample, distilled water.

## Procedure

**Test**

1. Dissolve the stated quantity of sample in 40 ml water in a Nessler cylinder (or use the solution as directed).
2. Add 2 ml of 20% w/v iron-free citric acid solution and 0.1 ml of thioglycollic acid; mix.
3. Make alkaline with iron-free ammonia solution (about 3–5 ml), dilute with water to 50 ml.
4. Allow to stand for 5 minutes.

**Standard**

5. Dilute the stated volume of iron standard solution with water to 40 ml in the second cylinder and treat exactly as the test (steps 2–4).

**Comparison**

6. View vertically against a **white background** and compare the purple colour.

## Observations

| Cylinder | Colour |
| --- | --- |
| Standard | Pale purple |
| Test | ___ |

## Result

The colour of the test is less / more intense than the standard; the sample **passes / fails** the limit test for iron.

## Precautions

1. Use iron-free reagents and avoid contact with metal spatulas.
2. Add reagents in the same order to both cylinders and wait the same time.
3. Make sure both solutions are alkaline.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is citric acid added?** To keep iron in solution as a complex, preventing precipitation of iron hydroxide in ammonia.
2. **Role of thioglycollic acid?** Reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and forms the purple ferrous thioglycollate complex.
3. **Why a white background?** Coloured solutions are compared best against white.
4. **Why is ammonia added?** The purple complex forms only in alkaline solution.
5. **Name the salt used for the iron standard.** Ferric ammonium sulphate.

# Limit test for arsenic

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for arsenic on the given sample by the Gutzeit method as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Arsenic compounds and arsine are highly poisonous. Work in a fume hood, keep the apparatus closed and follow your teacher's instructions. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Arsenic in the sample is reduced by **nascent hydrogen**, produced from arsenic-free **zinc and hydrochloric acid**, to **arsine gas (AsH3)**. Arsine passes up the tube and gives a **yellow to brown stain** on **mercuric chloride paper**. The stain from the sample is compared with that from a standard containing a known amount of arsenic.

- **Potassium iodide** and **stannous chloride** reduce pentavalent arsenic (As⁵⁺) to trivalent arsenic (As³⁺), which is converted to arsine faster and more completely; stannous chloride also helps steady evolution of hydrogen and deposits tin on zinc (activating it).
- **Stannated hydrochloric acid** (HCl containing a little stannous chloride) gives a steady reaction.
- **Lead acetate cotton wool** in the tube absorbs any hydrogen sulphide, which would otherwise darken the mercuric chloride paper.

## Requirements

Gutzeit apparatus (wide-mouthed bottle of about 120 ml, rubber bung, glass tube packed with lead acetate cotton wool, two flat-ended glass tubes holding mercuric chloride paper), water bath at 40 °C; arsenic-free (AsT) reagents: stannated hydrochloric acid, potassium iodide, stannous chloride solution, granulated zinc, mercuric chloride paper, standard arsenic solution, sample.

```text
        ___
       |   |  <- mercuric chloride paper between flat ends
       |___|
         |
         |   <- tube packed with lead acetate cotton wool
     ____|____
    |         |  <- bottle: sample + stannated HCl + KI + SnCl2 + zinc
    |_________|     40 °C, 40 minutes
```

## Procedure

**Test**

1. Place the sample solution (prepared as the monograph directs, usually in about 50 ml water) in the bottle.
2. Add 10 ml of stannated hydrochloric acid, 1 g of potassium iodide and 5 ml of stannous chloride solution.
3. Add 10 g of granulated zinc and immediately fit the bung with the tube assembly holding the lead acetate wool and the mercuric chloride paper.
4. Keep the bottle in a water bath at about **40 °C for 40 minutes**.

**Standard**

5. Repeat with the specified quantity of standard arsenic solution in place of the sample, using the same amounts of reagents and the same conditions.

**Comparison**

6. Remove the mercuric chloride papers and compare the stains at once.

## Observations

| Paper | Stain |
| --- | --- |
| Standard | Yellow-brown stain |
| Test | ___ (lighter / darker) |

## Result

The stain produced by the sample is lighter / darker than the standard stain. The sample **passes / fails** the limit test for arsenic.

## Precautions

1. Use only arsenic-free (AsT) reagents and zinc.
2. Keep the temperature at 40 °C; too fast evolution gives an uneven stain.
3. Make sure the lead acetate wool is not wet; the paper must be dry.
4. Compare stains immediately; they fade in light.
5. Never inhale the gas; work in a fume hood.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is lead acetate cotton wool used?** To absorb H2S, which would blacken the mercuric chloride paper.
2. **Role of KI and SnCl2?** Reduce As(V) to As(III) and keep hydrogen evolution steady.
3. **What gas causes the stain?** Arsine (AsH3).
4. **Why 40 °C?** For uniform, moderate evolution of hydrogen.
5. **What is the colour of the stain?** Yellow to brown.
6. **Why is arsenic tested separately from heavy metals?** It is very toxic at low levels and is not detected reliably by the sulphide-based heavy metals test.

# Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide

**Aim:** To prepare 1000 ml of approximately 0.1 M sodium hydroxide and standardise it using potassium hydrogen phthalate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Sodium hydroxide is corrosive. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Sodium hydroxide is not a primary standard: it is hygroscopic and absorbs carbon dioxide from air, so its exact strength is found by titration against **potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP)**, a primary standard (Mw 204.22).

KHC8H4O4 + NaOH → KNaC8H4O4 + H2O (1 : 1)

KHP is a weak acid, so the end point (about pH 9) is shown by **phenolphthalein** (colourless → pink).

**1 ml of 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 0.02042 g of KHP** (204.22 × 0.1/1000).

## Requirements

Sodium hydroxide pellets, potassium hydrogen phthalate (dried at 120 °C for 2 hours), phenolphthalein solution, freshly boiled and cooled (CO2-free) distilled water, analytical balance, 1000 ml volumetric flask, burette, conical flasks, weighing bottle; polythene bottle with a soda-lime guard tube for storage.

## Procedure

**Preparation**

1. Weigh about 4.2 g of NaOH (a little more than 4.0 g to allow for moisture and carbonate) quickly on a rough balance.
2. Dissolve in CO2-free water and make up to 1000 ml. For carbonate-free solution, a strong (about 50% w/v) NaOH solution can be allowed to stand so that Na2CO3 settles, and the clear liquid diluted.
3. Store in a well-closed polythene bottle.

**Standardisation**

4. Accurately weigh about 0.4 g of dried KHP into a conical flask.
5. Dissolve in about 50 ml of CO2-free water.
6. Add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein.
7. Titrate with the NaOH solution from the burette until a faint pink colour persists for 30 seconds.
8. Repeat to get three concordant readings (within 0.1 ml).

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of KHP (g) | Initial (ml) | Final (ml) | Volume of NaOH (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.4085 | 0.00 | 19.85 | 19.85 |
| 2 |  |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |  |

Molarity of NaOH = weight of KHP (g) / [volume (ml) × 0.2042]

Worked example: M = 0.4085/(19.85 × 0.2042) = 0.4085/4.0534 = **0.1008 M**.

Check by moles: 0.4085/204.22 = 0.002000 mol; 0.002000/0.01985 L = 0.1008 M.

Factor f = 0.1008/0.1 = 1.008.

## Result

The molarity of the given sodium hydroxide solution is ___ M (factor ___).

## Precautions

1. Use CO2-free water; carbonate makes the end point less sharp.
2. Do not use glass-stoppered bottles for NaOH (stoppers stick).
3. Rinse the burette with the NaOH solution before filling.
4. Take the first permanent faint pink as the end point; the pink fades slowly as CO2 is absorbed.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is NaOH a secondary standard?** It absorbs moisture and CO2, so its exact strength cannot be fixed by weighing.
2. **Why is KHP a good primary standard?** High purity, non-hygroscopic, stable, high equivalent weight.
3. **Why phenolphthalein?** The end point is near pH 9 (KHP is a weak acid), within 8.3–10.0.
4. **Can oxalic acid be used?** Yes; 1 ml 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 0.006303 g oxalic acid dihydrate.
5. **Why use CO2-free water?** Dissolved CO2 consumes NaOH and gives a fading end point.
practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide

# Preparation and standardisation of 0.05 M sulphuric acid

**Aim:** To prepare 1000 ml of approximately 0.05 M (0.1 N) sulphuric acid and standardise it with anhydrous sodium carbonate.

> Concentrated sulphuric acid is highly corrosive and gives out much heat with water. Always add acid to water slowly, never water to acid. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Concentrated H2SO4 does not have an exactly known strength and absorbs moisture, so a dilute solution is prepared approximately and standardised against **anhydrous sodium carbonate** (Mw 105.99), a primary standard.

Na2CO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2 (1 : 1)

Methyl orange (yellow → orange-pink) is used because the end point is in the acidic region; dissolved CO2 is removed by boiling near the end point.

**1 ml of 0.05 M H2SO4 ≡ 0.005299 g Na2CO3** (105.99 × 0.05/1000).

Because H2SO4 is dibasic, 0.05 M = 0.1 N.

## Requirements

Concentrated H2SO4 (about 98% w/w, density 1.84), anhydrous sodium carbonate (heated at about 270 °C for 1 hour and cooled in a desiccator), methyl orange, water, burette, conical flasks, 1000 ml volumetric flask, measuring cylinder, hot plate.

## Procedure

**Preparation**

1. Calculation: 0.05 mol × 98.08 = 4.904 g H2SO4; 4.904/0.98 = 5.0 g of concentrated acid; 5.0/1.84 ≈ **2.7 ml**. Take about 3 ml.
2. Add the acid slowly, with stirring, to about 800 ml water; cool and make up to 1000 ml.

**Standardisation**

3. Accurately weigh about 0.15 g of anhydrous Na2CO3 into a conical flask; dissolve in 50 ml water.
4. Add 2 drops of methyl orange.
5. Titrate with the acid until the colour just begins to change.
6. Boil gently for 2 minutes to expel CO2 (the colour returns to yellow), cool, and continue the titration to a permanent orange-pink.
7. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of Na2CO3 (g) | Volume of H2SO4 (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.1590 | 29.80 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

Expected volume for exactly 0.05 M = 0.1590/0.005299 = 30.01 ml.

f = 30.01/29.80 = 1.007; molarity = 0.05 × 1.007 = **0.05035 M** (normality 0.1007 N).

Check: moles Na2CO3 = 0.1590/105.99 = 0.001500; M = 0.001500/0.02980 = 0.05034 M.

## Result

The molarity of the sulphuric acid is ___ M (normality ___ N).

## Precautions

1. Add acid to water, never the reverse.
2. Dry the sodium carbonate properly; it is slightly hygroscopic.
3. Boil off CO2 near the end point for a sharp change.
4. Alternatively standardise against previously standardised NaOH using phenolphthalein.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the normality of 0.05 M H2SO4?** 0.1 N.
2. **Why boil near the end point?** CO2 forms carbonic acid, which changes the indicator early; boiling removes it.
3. **Why methyl orange and not phenolphthalein with Na2CO3?** Complete reaction to CO2 is shown only in the acidic range.
4. **Why is anhydrous Na2CO3 a primary standard?** Pure, stable, and can be dried to constant weight.
5. **Why add acid to water?** The heat produced is absorbed by the larger volume of water, preventing spurting.
practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of 0.05 M sulphuric acid

# Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate

**Aim:** To prepare 1000 ml of approximately 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate and standardise it using potassium bromate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Potassium bromate is toxic and an oxidiser. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Sodium thiosulphate (Na2S2O3·5H2O, Mw 248.18) is not a primary standard: it may be efflorescent, and its solutions are decomposed by bacteria, CO2 and light. It is standardised **iodometrically**: a known weight of **potassium bromate** (primary standard, Mw 167.00) liberates iodine from excess potassium iodide in acid, and the iodine is titrated with thiosulphate using starch.

KBrO3 + 6KI + 6HCl → 3I2 + KBr + 6KCl + 3H2O

I2 + 2Na2S2O3 → 2NaI + Na2S4O6

1 KBrO3 ≡ 3 I2 ≡ 6 Na2S2O3, so **1 ml of 0.1 M Na2S2O3 ≡ 0.002784 g KBrO3** (167.00 × 0.1/6/1000 = 0.002783; IP figure 0.002784).

## Requirements

Sodium thiosulphate pentahydrate, sodium carbonate, potassium bromate (dried), potassium iodide, 2 M (or dilute) HCl, starch solution (freshly prepared), freshly boiled and cooled water, iodine flasks (stoppered), burette, 250 ml volumetric flask, pipettes.

## Procedure

**Preparation**

1. Dissolve about 25 g of Na2S2O3·5H2O and 0.2 g of Na2CO3 in freshly boiled and cooled water and make up to 1000 ml. (Na2CO3 keeps the pH slightly alkaline; boiled water is free from CO2 and bacteria.)
2. Keep in an amber bottle; standardise after a day.

**Standardisation**

3. Accurately weigh about 0.2 g of dried KBrO3, dissolve in water and make up to 250 ml in a volumetric flask.
4. Pipette 50 ml into an iodine flask; add 2 g of KI and 3 ml of 2 M HCl; stopper and keep in the dark for about 5 minutes.
5. Titrate the liberated iodine with the thiosulphate solution until the colour is pale straw yellow.
6. Add 1–2 ml of starch solution (blue colour) and continue until the blue just disappears.
7. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

KBrO3 weighed = 0.2000 g in 250 ml → 50 ml contains 0.04000 g.

| Trial | Volume of thiosulphate (ml) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 14.30 |
| 2 |  |
| 3 |  |

Expected volume for exactly 0.1 M = 0.04000/0.002784 = 14.37 ml.

f = 14.37/14.30 = 1.005; molarity = **0.1005 M**.

Alternative standard: potassium dichromate (Cr2O7²⁻ + 6I⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I2 + 7H2O); 1 ml of 0.1 M thiosulphate ≡ 0.004903 g K2Cr2O7.

## Result

The molarity of the sodium thiosulphate solution is ___ M.

## Precautions

1. Add starch only near the end point (pale yellow).
2. Use stoppered flasks and keep in the dark before titration (iodine loss, air oxidation of iodide).
3. Do not let the solution become strongly acidic during titration.
4. Use fresh starch solution.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is Na2CO3 added to the thiosulphate solution?** To keep it slightly alkaline and stable against CO2 and bacteria.
2. **Why boiled water?** To remove CO2 and kill bacteria that decompose thiosulphate.
3. **Why is starch added late?** Large amounts of iodine bind strongly to starch and are released slowly, giving a late end point.
4. **Is this iodimetry or iodometry?** Iodometry (titration of liberated iodine).
5. **Equivalent weight of KBrO3 here?** Mw/6 = 27.83.
practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate

practicals.markdown:
# Preparation and standardisation of 0.02 M potassium permanganate

**Aim:** To prepare 1000 ml of approximately 0.02 M (0.1 N) potassium permanganate and standardise it with oxalic acid.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves; handle hot solutions with care.

## Principle

KMnO4 is not a primary standard (it contains some MnO2, and its solutions are decomposed by light, heat and organic matter). It is standardised against **oxalic acid dihydrate** (H2C2O4·2H2O, Mw 126.07) in dilute **sulphuric acid** at 60–70 °C.

2MnO4⁻ + 5C2O4²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO2 + 8H2O

The reaction is slow at first and speeds up as Mn²⁺ forms (**autocatalysis**). KMnO4 acts as its **own indicator**: the first permanent pink marks the end point.

In acid, n = 5 for permanganate, so 0.02 M = 0.1 N. For oxalic acid n = 2.

**1 ml of 0.02 M KMnO4 ≡ 0.006303 g H2C2O4·2H2O** (126.07/2 × 0.1/1000).

## Requirements

KMnO4, oxalic acid dihydrate (AR), dilute sulphuric acid, distilled water, beakers, glass wool, amber bottle, burette (glass stopcock), conical flasks, thermometer, water bath or hot plate.

## Procedure

**Preparation**

1. Weigh about 3.2 g of KMnO4 (0.02 × 158.03 = 3.16 g), dissolve in 1000 ml water.
2. Heat on a water bath for about an hour (or boil for 15 minutes), cover and keep for 2 days to oxidise organic matter.
3. Filter through glass wool (not filter paper, which reduces permanganate) into an amber bottle.

**Standardisation**

4. Accurately weigh about 0.15–0.16 g oxalic acid dihydrate into a conical flask.
5. Dissolve in 50 ml water and add 20 ml of dilute H2SO4.
6. Warm to 60–70 °C.
7. Titrate with KMnO4 slowly at first (wait for each drop to decolourise), then faster, to a faint pink that persists for 30 seconds.
8. Repeat for concordant readings. Read the upper meniscus (the solution is deeply coloured).

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of oxalic acid (g) | Volume of KMnO4 (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.1600 | 25.20 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

Expected volume for exactly 0.02 M = 0.1600/0.006303 = 25.38 ml.

f = 25.38/25.20 = 1.007; molarity = 0.02 × 1.007 = **0.02014 M** (0.1007 N).

## Result

The molarity of the potassium permanganate solution is ___ M.

## Precautions

1. Use H2SO4 only — HCl is oxidised to chlorine, HNO3 is itself an oxidant.
2. Keep the temperature at 60–70 °C; above about 80 °C oxalic acid decomposes.
3. A brown precipitate (MnO2) means too little acid or too fast addition.
4. Use a burette with a glass stopcock (permanganate attacks rubber).
5. Read the upper meniscus.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is KMnO4 a self-indicator?** MnO4⁻ is intensely purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless; one excess drop gives pink.
2. **Why heat the oxalic acid solution?** The reaction is slow at room temperature.
3. **What is autocatalysis?** A product (Mn²⁺) catalyses the reaction, so it speeds up once started.
4. **Why filter through glass wool?** Paper reduces permanganate to MnO2.
5. **What is the normality of 0.02 M KMnO4 in acid?** 0.1 N.
practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of 0.02 M potassium permanganate

# Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate

**Aim:** To prepare 1000 ml of approximately 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate and standardise it against arsenic trioxide.

> Arsenic trioxide is highly poisonous and osmic acid (osmium tetroxide) is toxic and volatile. Use only under supervision, in a fume hood, with gloves and goggles. Your lab may use ferrous ammonium sulphate standardisation instead.

## Principle

Ceric ions are a strong one-electron oxidant in sulphuric acid:

Ce⁴⁺ + e⁻ → Ce³⁺ (n = 1, so 0.1 M = 0.1 N)

Ceric ammonium sulphate is standardised against **arsenic trioxide** (As2O3, Mw 197.84), a primary standard. As2O3 is dissolved in sodium hydroxide (as arsenite), acidified, and titrated with the ceric solution. The reaction is slow, so a trace of **osmic acid** is added as a catalyst. **Ferroin** shows the end point (pink/red → pale blue).

2Ce⁴⁺ + As³⁺ → 2Ce³⁺ + As⁵⁺ (each As loses 2 electrons; As2O3 contains 2 As → 4 electrons)

**1 ml of 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate ≡ 0.004946 g As2O3** (197.84/4 × 0.1/1000).

## Requirements

Ceric ammonium sulphate, concentrated sulphuric acid, arsenic trioxide (dried at 105 °C), sodium hydroxide solution (about 8% w/v), dilute sulphuric acid, osmic acid solution, ferroin solution, burette, conical flasks, 1000 ml volumetric flask.

## Procedure

**Preparation**

1. Dissolve about 65 g of ceric ammonium sulphate, with gentle heat, in a mixture of 30 ml concentrated H2SO4 and about 500 ml water.
2. Cool, filter if turbid, and make up to 1000 ml with water.

**Standardisation**

3. Accurately weigh about 0.2 g of As2O3 into a conical flask.
4. Add 25 ml of 8% w/v NaOH solution and swirl to dissolve.
5. Add 100 ml water and 30 ml dilute H2SO4.
6. Add 0.15 ml of osmic acid solution and 0.1 ml of ferroin.
7. Titrate with the ceric solution until the pink colour changes to a very pale blue. Add the titrant slowly near the end.
8. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of As2O3 (g) | Volume of ceric solution (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.2000 | 40.20 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

Expected volume for exactly 0.1 M = 0.2000/0.004946 = 40.44 ml.

f = 40.44/40.20 = 1.006; molarity = **0.1006 M**.

## Result

The molarity of the ceric ammonium sulphate solution is ___ M.

## Precautions

1. Handle As2O3 and osmic acid with extreme care; dispose of waste as directed.
2. Keep the ceric solution strongly acidic; ceric salts hydrolyse in weak acid.
3. Add titrant slowly near the end point for a sharp change.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is osmic acid added?** It catalyses the slow reaction between Ce⁴⁺ and arsenite.
2. **Colour change of ferroin?** Red/pink (ferrous form) → pale blue (ferric form).
3. **Why is ceric sulphate stable?** It does not decompose on standing or boiling, unlike permanganate.
4. **Can ceric titrations be done in HCl?** Yes, chloride is not oxidised in the cold.
5. **What other standard can be used?** Ferrous ammonium sulphate (standardised) or sodium oxalate.
practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate

# Assay of ammonium chloride by acid–base (formol) titration

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of ammonium chloride by the formol titration and to standardise the sodium hydroxide used.

> Formaldehyde is irritant and toxic. Use it in a fume hood. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

The ammonium ion is too weak an acid (pKa about 9.25) to be titrated sharply with NaOH. **Formaldehyde** reacts with ammonium chloride to form hexamethylenetetramine and liberates an equivalent amount of hydrochloric acid, which is titrated with standard NaOH using **phenolphthalein**:

4NH4Cl + 6HCHO → (CH2)6N4 + 4HCl + 6H2O

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O

So 1 NH4Cl ≡ 1 HCl ≡ 1 NaOH. **1 ml of 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 0.005349 g NH4Cl** (Mw 53.49).

Formaldehyde usually contains formic acid, so it is **neutralised to phenolphthalein** before use.

## Requirements

Ammonium chloride sample, formaldehyde solution (about 37%), phenolphthalein, 0.1 M NaOH, potassium hydrogen phthalate (for standardising NaOH), burette, pipettes, conical flasks, analytical balance.

## Procedure

**Standardisation of 0.1 M NaOH** — against potassium hydrogen phthalate with phenolphthalein, as described in the NaOH standardisation guide (1 ml of 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 0.02042 g KHP).

**Neutralised formaldehyde** — take about 25 ml formaldehyde solution, add a few drops of phenolphthalein, and add 0.1 M NaOH dropwise to a faint pink.

**Assay**

1. Accurately weigh about 0.1 g of ammonium chloride; dissolve in 20 ml water in a conical flask.
2. Add 5 ml of the neutralised formaldehyde solution; mix and allow to stand for 2 minutes.
3. Add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein (if not already present).
4. Titrate with 0.1 M NaOH to a faint pink that persists for 30 seconds.
5. Repeat for concordant results.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of NH4Cl (g) | Volume of 0.1 M NaOH (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.1050 | 19.55 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

Factor of NaOH (f) = 1.004 (from standardisation).

% NH4Cl = V × f × 0.005349 × 100 / w

Worked example: 19.55 × 1.004 × 0.005349 × 100 / 0.1050 = 0.10499 × 100 / 0.1050 = **100.0%** (on the dried basis).

## Result

The percentage purity of the given ammonium chloride is ___% w/w.

## Precautions

1. Neutralise the formaldehyde before use; otherwise its formic acid adds to the titre.
2. Allow time for the reaction before titrating.
3. Use CO2-free water.
4. Work with formaldehyde in a fume hood.

## Viva questions

1. **Why can't NH4Cl be titrated directly with NaOH?** NH4⁺ is a very weak acid; no sharp end point.
2. **What is formed with formaldehyde?** Hexamine and an equivalent amount of HCl.
3. **Why neutralise the formaldehyde?** It contains formic acid, which would give a high result.
4. **Another method?** Boil with excess standard NaOH to drive off ammonia and back-titrate the excess with standard acid.
5. **Which indicator and why?** Phenolphthalein; the end point is in the slightly alkaline region.
practicals.title: Assay of ammonium chloride by acid–base (formol) titration

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of ferrous sulphate by cerimetry

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of ferrous sulphate (FeSO4·7H2O) by titration with 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Ferrous ions are oxidised to ferric ions by ceric ions in sulphuric acid solution:

Fe²⁺ + Ce⁴⁺ → Fe³⁺ + Ce³⁺ (1 : 1)

**Ferroin** (1,10-phenanthroline ferrous sulphate) is the indicator: it stays red while Fe²⁺ is present and is oxidised to pale blue by the first excess Ce⁴⁺.

**1 ml of 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate ≡ 0.02780 g FeSO4·7H2O** (Mw 278.01).

Freshly boiled and cooled water and acid are used so that dissolved oxygen does not oxidise Fe²⁺ before titration.

## Requirements

Ferrous sulphate sample, 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate (standardised), dilute sulphuric acid, freshly boiled and cooled water, ferroin solution, burette, conical flasks, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Standardise the ceric ammonium sulphate solution (see its guide).
2. Accurately weigh about 0.5 g of ferrous sulphate.
3. Dissolve in a mixture of 30 ml dilute H2SO4 and 20 ml freshly boiled and cooled water.
4. Add 1–2 drops of ferroin.
5. Titrate immediately with 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate until the red colour changes to pale blue (greenish-blue).
6. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of FeSO4·7H2O (g) | Volume of ceric solution (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.5000 | 17.85 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

f (ceric) = 1.002.

% FeSO4·7H2O = V × f × 0.02780 × 100 / w

Worked example: 17.85 × 1.002 × 0.02780 × 100 / 0.5000 = 0.4972 × 100/0.5000 = **99.4%**.

## Result

The given sample contains ___% w/w of FeSO4·7H2O.

## Precautions

1. Titrate soon after dissolving; Fe²⁺ is slowly oxidised by air.
2. Use boiled and cooled water.
3. Add the indicator just before titration and titrate slowly near the end.
4. Crystals that have turned brown (oxidised) give low results.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is ferroin used?** It changes sharply from red to pale blue at a potential (about 1.1 V) between those of Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ and Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺.
2. **Why boiled water?** To remove dissolved oxygen, which oxidises Fe²⁺.
3. **Why sulphuric acid?** Ceric salts must be kept acidic to avoid hydrolysis; it also stabilises Fe²⁺.
4. **Equivalent weight of FeSO4·7H2O here?** Its molecular weight, 278.01 (one electron).
5. **Advantage of cerimetry over permanganometry for this assay?** Stable titrant, can be used with HCl, single electron change.
practicals.title: Assay of ferrous sulphate by cerimetry

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of copper sulphate by iodometry

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of copper sulphate (CuSO4·5H2O) by iodometric titration with 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Cupric ions oxidise iodide in weakly acid solution, forming white cuprous iodide and liberating iodine:

2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I2

The iodine is titrated with standard sodium thiosulphate using starch:

I2 + 2S2O3²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S4O6²⁻

2Cu ≡ I2 ≡ 2S2O3²⁻, so Cu : thiosulphate = 1 : 1. **1 ml of 0.1 M Na2S2O3 ≡ 0.02497 g CuSO4·5H2O** (Mw 249.68).

**Acetic acid** keeps the solution weakly acidic (strong mineral acid would let air oxidise iodide; alkali would precipitate copper hydroxide). **Potassium thiocyanate**, added near the end, converts CuI to the less soluble CuSCN and releases iodine adsorbed on the precipitate.

## Requirements

Copper sulphate sample, potassium iodide, acetic acid, potassium thiocyanate, starch solution, 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate (standardised), iodine flask, burette, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Standardise the thiosulphate (see its guide).
2. Accurately weigh about 1 g of copper sulphate into an iodine flask; dissolve in 50 ml water.
3. Add 5 ml of acetic acid and 3 g of potassium iodide; stopper, mix and keep for 2–3 minutes.
4. Titrate the liberated iodine with 0.1 M thiosulphate until the brown colour becomes pale yellow (the white CuI precipitate is visible).
5. Add 2 ml of starch solution (blue) and about 1 g of potassium thiocyanate (or 10 ml of its solution); the blue deepens as adsorbed iodine is released.
6. Continue titrating until the blue disappears, leaving a creamy white precipitate.
7. Repeat for concordant results.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight of CuSO4·5H2O (g) | Volume of thiosulphate (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1.000 | 39.60 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

f (thiosulphate) = 1.004.

% CuSO4·5H2O = V × f × 0.02497 × 100 / w

Worked example: 39.60 × 1.004 × 0.02497 × 100 / 1.000 = **99.3%**.

## Result

The given sample contains ___% w/w of CuSO4·5H2O.

## Precautions

1. Use excess KI and a stoppered flask to avoid loss of iodine.
2. Add starch only near the end point.
3. Add KSCN only near the end; added early it can reduce some iodine.
4. Do not use strong mineral acid.

## Viva questions

1. **Is this iodimetry or iodometry?** Iodometry — liberated iodine is titrated.
2. **Why add KSCN?** To release iodine adsorbed on CuI by converting it to CuSCN.
3. **What is the white precipitate?** Cuprous iodide (CuI), later CuSCN.
4. **Why acetic acid?** To keep the solution weakly acidic without oxidation of iodide by air.
5. **Equivalent weight of CuSO4·5H2O here?** Molecular weight, 249.68 (one electron per Cu).
practicals.title: Assay of copper sulphate by iodometry

# Assay of calcium gluconate by complexometric titration

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of calcium gluconate by complexometric titration with 0.05 M disodium edetate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Calcium ions form a stable 1 : 1 complex with EDTA at pH 10:

Ca²⁺ + H2Y²⁻ → CaY²⁻ + 2H⁺

The end point is shown by **Eriochrome Black T (mordant black 11)**: wine red (metal complex) → blue (free indicator). Calcium alone gives a poor, gradual colour change with this indicator because the Ca–indicator complex is weak. A small, known volume of **0.05 M magnesium sulphate** is added; magnesium forms a stronger red complex with the indicator, and at the end point EDTA removes the Mg from the indicator, giving a sharp change. The volume of MgSO4 added is subtracted from the titre.

**1 ml of 0.05 M disodium edetate ≡ 0.02242 g C12H22CaO14·H2O** (Mw 448.4).

**Standardisation of 0.05 M disodium edetate:** dissolve about 18.6 g of disodium edetate (Mw 372.24) to 1000 ml; standardise against granulated zinc dissolved in dilute HCl, buffered to pH 10, with Eriochrome Black T (1 ml 0.05 M ≡ 0.003269 g Zn).

## Requirements

Calcium gluconate sample, 0.05 M disodium edetate (standardised), 0.05 M magnesium sulphate, strong ammonia–ammonium chloride buffer (pH about 10), mordant black 11 mixture, burette, conical flasks, water bath.

## Procedure

1. Accurately weigh about 0.5 g calcium gluconate; dissolve in 50 ml warm water; cool.
2. Add exactly 5.0 ml of 0.05 M magnesium sulphate solution.
3. Add 10 ml of strong ammonia–ammonium chloride buffer.
4. Add about 0.1 g of mordant black 11 mixture (wine red colour).
5. Titrate with 0.05 M disodium edetate until the colour changes to a clear blue.
6. Subtract 5.0 ml (the volume of 0.05 M MgSO4 added) from the burette reading.
7. Repeat for concordant results.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Weight (g) | Burette reading (ml) | Net volume (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.4980 | 27.10 | 22.10 |
| 2 |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |

f (EDTA) = 1.003.

% = (V − 5.0) × f × 0.02242 × 100 / w

Worked example: 22.10 × 1.003 × 0.02242 × 100 / 0.4980 = 0.4970 × 100/0.4980 = **99.8%**.

## Result

The given sample contains ___% w/w of calcium gluconate monohydrate.

## Precautions

1. Cool the solution before adding the buffer.
2. Measure the MgSO4 solution exactly; its strength must match the EDTA molarity (or correct for it).
3. Titrate slowly near the end point; the change from violet to blue is gradual at the last drops.
4. Use a fresh indicator mixture.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is MgSO4 added?** Calcium gives a poor end point with Eriochrome Black T; magnesium gives a sharp wine red → blue change.
2. **Why is it subtracted?** The added Mg also consumes EDTA.
3. **Why pH 10?** Ca– and Mg–EDTA complexes are stable at this pH and the indicator works in this range.
4. **Ratio of metal to EDTA?** Always 1 : 1.
5. **Another indicator for calcium?** Hydroxynaphthol blue (or calcon) at pH 12–13.
practicals.title: Assay of calcium gluconate by complexometry

# Assay of hydrogen peroxide by permanganometry

**Aim:** To determine the strength of hydrogen peroxide solution (% w/v and volume strength) by titration with 0.02 M potassium permanganate.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Concentrated hydrogen peroxide burns skin. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

In sulphuric acid solution, hydrogen peroxide acts as a reducing agent towards permanganate and is oxidised to oxygen:

2MnO4⁻ + 5H2O2 + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O2 + 8H2O

KMnO4 is its own indicator (first permanent pink). For H2O2, n = 2; 0.02 M KMnO4 is 0.1 N.

**1 ml of 0.02 M KMnO4 ≡ 0.001701 g H2O2** (34.01/2 × 0.1/1000).

**Volume strength:** 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. 68.02 g H2O2 gives 22.4 L O2 at STP, so 1 g gives about 0.329 L. Volume strength = (g of H2O2 per litre) × 0.329.

## Requirements

Hydrogen peroxide solution (about 3% or 6% w/v), 0.02 M KMnO4 (standardised against oxalic acid), dilute sulphuric acid, 100 ml volumetric flask, pipettes (10 ml), burette, conical flasks.

## Procedure

1. Standardise the KMnO4 solution (see its guide).
2. Pipette 10 ml of the hydrogen peroxide solution into a 100 ml volumetric flask and dilute to the mark with water; mix.
3. Pipette 10 ml of the diluted solution (= 1 ml of original) into a conical flask.
4. Add 20 ml of dilute H2SO4 (do not heat).
5. Titrate with 0.02 M KMnO4 to the first permanent faint pink.
6. Repeat for concordant results.

## Observations and calculation

| Trial | Volume of diluted H2O2 (ml) | Volume of 0.02 M KMnO4 (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 10.0 | 17.60 |
| 2 | 10.0 |  |
| 3 | 10.0 |  |

f (KMnO4) = 1.008.

H2O2 in 1 ml of original solution = 17.60 × 1.008 × 0.001701 = 0.03018 g.

% w/v = 0.03018 × 100 = **3.02% w/v**.

g per litre = 30.18; volume strength = 30.18 × 0.329 = **9.9, about 10 volumes**.

## Result

The hydrogen peroxide solution contains ___% w/v H2O2 (about ___ volume strength).

## Precautions

1. Do not warm the solution; H2O2 decomposes on heating.
2. Use sulphuric acid only.
3. Pipette H2O2 with a pipette filler; never by mouth.
4. Keep the stock bottle closed and cool.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is H2O2 a reducing agent here?** Permanganate is a stronger oxidant; H2O2 gives up electrons and is oxidised to O2.
2. **What does "20 volume" mean?** 1 ml releases 20 ml of oxygen at STP; about 6% w/v.
3. **Why dilute the sample first?** To bring the titre into a convenient range.
4. **Why is no heating done here, unlike with oxalate?** The reaction is fast and H2O2 decomposes on heating.
5. **What other method can assay H2O2?** Iodometry (H2O2 + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I2 + 2H2O) or cerimetry.
practicals.title: Assay of hydrogen peroxide by permanganometry

# Assay of sodium benzoate by non-aqueous titration

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of sodium benzoate by non-aqueous titration with 0.1 M perchloric acid.

> Perchloric acid is corrosive and can react violently with organic matter when concentrated or heated. Glacial acetic acid and acetic anhydride are corrosive and irritant. Work in a fume hood. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

The benzoate ion is a very weak base in water and cannot be titrated sharply there. In **glacial acetic acid** (a protogenic solvent) its basic character is enhanced, and it is titrated with **perchloric acid**, the strongest acid in this medium:

HClO4 + CH3COOH → CH3COOH2⁺ + ClO4⁻

C6H5COO⁻ + CH3COOH2⁺ → C6H5COOH + CH3COOH

Overall: C6H5COONa + HClO4 → C6H5COOH + NaClO4 (1 : 1).

**1 ml of 0.1 M HClO4 ≡ 0.01441 g C7H5NaO2** (Mw 144.10).

**Standardisation of 0.1 M HClO4:** against potassium hydrogen phthalate dissolved in glacial acetic acid, crystal violet indicator; 1 ml of 0.1 M HClO4 ≡ 0.02042 g KHP.

## Requirements

Sodium benzoate (dried), 0.1 M perchloric acid in glacial acetic acid (prepared with acetic anhydride to remove water), anhydrous glacial acetic acid, potassium hydrogen phthalate, crystal violet solution (or 1-naphtholbenzein, as directed), dry burette and dry glassware, warm water bath, thermometer.

## Procedure

**Standardisation**

1. Accurately weigh about 0.35 g KHP; dissolve in 50 ml glacial acetic acid (warm if needed, cool).
2. Add 2 drops of crystal violet; titrate with 0.1 M HClO4 from violet to blue-green (emerald green).
3. Run a blank with the solvent alone and subtract it. Note the temperature.

**Assay**

4. Accurately weigh about 0.25 g of dried sodium benzoate into a dry conical flask.
5. Add 20 ml of anhydrous glacial acetic acid; warm gently to dissolve; cool to room temperature.
6. Add the indicator.
7. Titrate with 0.1 M HClO4 to the end-point colour (violet → blue-green with crystal violet).
8. Carry out a blank titration and subtract.

## Observations and calculation

Standardisation: 0.3500 g KHP used 17.05 ml (blank negligible). Expected = 0.3500/0.02042 = 17.14 ml; f = 17.14/17.05 = **1.005**.

| Trial | Weight of sodium benzoate (g) | Titre (ml) | Blank (ml) | Net (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.2510 | 17.30 | 0.10 | 17.20 |
| 2 |  |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |  |

% = (V − blank) × f × 0.01441 × 100 / w = 17.20 × 1.005 × 0.01441 × 100 / 0.2510 = **99.2%**.

**Temperature correction** (if the titration temperature t2 differs from the standardisation temperature t1): corrected M = M × [1 + 0.0011 (t1 − t2)].

## Result

The percentage purity of the given sodium benzoate is ___% (on the dried basis).

## Precautions

1. All glassware must be dry; water spoils the end point.
2. Keep the perchloric acid solution away from heat and organic waste.
3. Do the blank and correct for temperature.
4. Cool the solution before titrating.

## Viva questions

1. **Why can't sodium benzoate be titrated in water with HCl?** Benzoate is too weak a base in water; no sharp end point.
2. **Why glacial acetic acid?** It is a protogenic solvent that enhances the basicity of weak bases.
3. **Why acetic anhydride in the titrant?** To react with water present in perchloric acid and the solvent.
4. **Why is a blank needed?** To correct for titrant used by the solvent and indicator.
5. **Why is temperature important?** Acetic acid expands considerably with temperature, changing molarity.
practicals.title: Assay of sodium benzoate by non-aqueous titration

# Assay of sodium chloride by precipitation titration (Mohr's method)

**Aim:** To standardise 0.1 M silver nitrate and determine the percentage purity of sodium chloride by Mohr's method.

> Silver nitrate stains skin and clothes and is irritant; potassium chromate is toxic. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Chloride is titrated with silver nitrate in neutral solution, with **potassium chromate** as indicator:

Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl (white precipitate)

When all chloride has precipitated, the first excess of silver ion forms **red-brown silver chromate**:

2Ag⁺ + CrO4²⁻ → Ag2CrO4 (red-brown)

Silver chloride precipitates first because it needs a much lower silver ion concentration to reach its solubility product. The solution must be neutral or faintly alkaline (pH about 6.5–9).

**1 ml of 0.1 M AgNO3 ≡ 0.005844 g NaCl** (Mw 58.44).

## Requirements

Silver nitrate (about 17 g per litre for 0.1 M), sodium chloride (dried at 130 °C, primary standard grade), sodium chloride sample, potassium chromate solution (5% w/v), amber burette or bottle, conical flasks, analytical balance.

## Procedure

**Standardisation of 0.1 M AgNO3**

1. Accurately weigh about 0.1 g of dried primary-standard NaCl; dissolve in 50 ml water.
2. Add 1 ml of potassium chromate solution.
3. Titrate with AgNO3, swirling constantly, until a faint permanent reddish-brown tinge appears in the yellow suspension.
4. Do an indicator blank: 50 ml water + 1 ml chromate + a little CaCO3 (to imitate the white precipitate); titrate to the same tint and subtract.

**Assay**

5. Accurately weigh about 0.1 g of the sample; dissolve in 50 ml water.
6. Add 1 ml potassium chromate solution and titrate with standardised AgNO3 as above.
7. Repeat for concordant results.

## Observations and calculation

Standardisation: 0.1000 g NaCl used 17.05 ml (blank 0.05 ml); net 17.00 ml. Expected = 0.1000/0.005844 = 17.11 ml; f = 17.11/17.00 = **1.006**.

| Trial | Weight of sample (g) | Net volume of AgNO3 (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.1012 | 17.15 |
| 2 |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |

% NaCl = V × f × 0.005844 × 100 / w = 17.15 × 1.006 × 0.005844 × 100 / 0.1012 = **99.6%**.

## Result

The molarity of silver nitrate is ___ M, and the sample contains ___% NaCl.

## Precautions

1. Keep pH between about 6.5 and 9; neutralise acidic samples with sodium bicarbonate or borax.
2. Swirl constantly; local excess of Ag⁺ gives a premature red colour.
3. Store AgNO3 in amber bottles; avoid direct light.
4. Do the indicator blank.
5. Collect silver residues for recovery.

## Viva questions

1. **Why must the solution be neutral?** In acid, chromate becomes dichromate and the end point is late; in alkali, silver oxide precipitates.
2. **Why does AgCl precipitate before Ag2CrO4?** Its solubility product is reached at a much lower silver ion concentration.
3. **Why is an indicator blank needed?** A small excess of Ag⁺ is required before the red colour is visible.
4. **Can Mohr's method be used for iodide?** No, AgI adsorbs chromate and the end point is unclear.
5. **Name two other methods for chloride.** Volhard's (back titration with thiocyanate and ferric alum) and Fajans' (adsorption indicator).
practicals.title: Assay of sodium chloride by precipitation titration

# Conductometric titration of strong acid against strong base

**Aim:** To determine the normality (molarity) of the given hydrochloric acid by conductometric titration with standard sodium hydroxide.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

Conductance of a solution depends on the number and mobility of its ions. H⁺ (about 350 S cm² mol⁻¹) and OH⁻ (about 198) are much faster than Na⁺ (about 50) and Cl⁻ (about 76).

H⁺ + Cl⁻ + Na⁺ + OH⁻ → Na⁺ + Cl⁻ + H2O

- Before the end point, fast H⁺ is replaced by slow Na⁺, so conductance **falls**.
- After the end point, excess Na⁺ and fast OH⁻ are added, so conductance **rises** steeply.

A plot of conductance against volume of NaOH gives two straight lines (V shape); their **intersection** is the end point. No indicator is needed.

N(HCl) × V(HCl) = N(NaOH) × V(NaOH at end point)

## Requirements

Conductivity meter (or bridge) with a dip-type cell (platinised platinum electrodes), 0.1 N NaOH (standardised), the HCl sample (about 0.01 N), standard 0.01 M KCl (to check the cell constant), 100 ml beaker, magnetic stirrer, burette, pipette, graph paper.

## Procedure

1. Switch on the conductivity meter, let it warm up and calibrate/check the cell constant with standard KCl solution as directed.
2. Pipette 50 ml of the HCl solution into a clean beaker (dilute with water if needed so that the electrodes are covered).
3. Dip the conductivity cell, stir gently and record the initial conductance.
4. Add 0.1 N NaOH from the burette in 0.5 ml portions; stir, wait for a steady reading and record the conductance after each addition.
5. Continue until about 8–10 readings have been taken past the minimum.
6. Plot conductance (y-axis) against volume of NaOH (x-axis). Draw the best straight lines through the falling and rising points; read the volume at their intersection.

## Observations and calculation

| Volume of 0.1 N NaOH (ml) | Conductance (mS) |
| --- | --- |
| 0.0 |  |
| 0.5 |  |
| 1.0 |  |
| ... |  |

Correction for dilution (if the titrant is not much stronger than the sample): corrected G = observed G × (V + v)/V, where V is the initial volume and v the volume added.

**Worked example:** 50 ml HCl; lines intersect at 5.20 ml of 0.1000 N NaOH.

N(HCl) = 0.1000 × 5.20 / 50 = **0.0104 N** (0.0104 M). Strength = 0.0104 × 36.46 = 0.379 g/L.

## Result

The normality of the given hydrochloric acid is ___ N.

## Precautions

1. Keep the temperature constant; conductance changes about 2% per °C.
2. Rinse the cell with distilled water and then with the sample; do not touch the platinum plates.
3. Use a titrant about 10 times more concentrated than the sample to keep volume change small.
4. Stir after each addition and read only when steady.
5. Use points away from the end point to draw the lines.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does conductance fall at first?** Highly mobile H⁺ ions are replaced by slower Na⁺ ions.
2. **Why does it rise after the end point?** Excess NaOH adds fast OH⁻ ions.
3. **Why is AC used?** DC would electrolyse the solution and polarise the electrodes.
4. **What is the cell constant?** l/A of the cell; κ = G × cell constant.
5. **Advantage over indicator titration?** Works for coloured, turbid or very dilute solutions; no indicator error.
practicals.title: Conductometric titration of strong acid against strong base

practicals.markdown:
# Conductometric titration of strong acid and weak acid against strong base

**Aim:** To determine the normality of hydrochloric acid and acetic acid in a mixture by conductometric titration with standard sodium hydroxide.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

In the mixture, the strong acid (HCl) is fully ionised and its H⁺ suppresses the ionisation of the weak acid (CH3COOH). On adding NaOH:

1. **Strong acid neutralised first:** fast H⁺ replaced by slow Na⁺ → conductance **falls steeply** → first break (end point of HCl).
2. **Weak acid neutralised next:** CH3COOH (poorly ionised) becomes CH3COO⁻ Na⁺ (fully ionised) → conductance **rises slowly** → second break (end point of acetic acid).
3. **Excess NaOH:** fast OH⁻ ions → conductance **rises steeply**.

```text
 G
 |\                        /
 | \                      /   excess NaOH
 |  \               _____/
 |   \        _____/          acetic acid neutralised
 |    \______/
 |    HCl neutralised
 +-----|-----------|--------- volume of NaOH
      V1          V2
```

N(HCl) = N(NaOH) × V1 / V(sample); N(CH3COOH) = N(NaOH) × (V2 − V1) / V(sample).

## Requirements

Conductivity meter and cell, standardised 0.1 N NaOH, the acid mixture (each acid about 0.005–0.01 N), beaker, magnetic stirrer, burette, pipette, graph paper.

## Procedure

1. Check the meter and cell constant with standard KCl as directed.
2. Pipette 50 ml of the acid mixture into a beaker; dip the cell; record the initial conductance.
3. Add 0.1 N NaOH in 0.5 ml portions, stirring and recording the steady conductance after each addition.
4. Continue well past the second break (until the steep rise is clear for 5–6 points).
5. Plot conductance against volume; draw three straight lines and note the two intersection volumes V1 and V2.

## Observations and calculation

| Volume of 0.1 N NaOH (ml) | Conductance (mS) |
| --- | --- |
| 0.0 |  |
| 0.5 |  |
| ... |  |

**Worked example:** 50 ml mixture; V1 = 2.60 ml, V2 = 5.80 ml of 0.1000 N NaOH.

- HCl: 0.1000 × 2.60/50 = **0.0052 N**.
- Acetic acid: 0.1000 × (5.80 − 2.60)/50 = 0.1000 × 3.20/50 = **0.0064 N** (0.0064 × 60.05 = 0.384 g/L).

## Result

The mixture contains HCl ___ N and acetic acid ___ N.

## Precautions

1. Constant temperature throughout.
2. Small, equal additions near the two breaks.
3. Use a concentrated titrant or apply the dilution correction G × (V + v)/V.
4. Draw straight lines using points away from each break.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the HCl neutralised first?** It is the stronger acid; its H⁺ also suppresses ionisation of acetic acid.
2. **Why does conductance rise slowly in the second stage?** Weakly ionised acetic acid is converted to fully ionised sodium acetate, but Na⁺ and acetate are slow ions.
3. **Can this mixture be titrated with indicators?** Not accurately; two end points are not seen sharply with indicators.
4. **What would NH4OH as titrant show after the end point?** A nearly flat line, since excess weak base hardly ionises.
5. **State Kohlrausch's law.** At infinite dilution, molar conductance = sum of limiting ionic conductances of cation and anion.
practicals.title: Conductometric titration of strong acid and weak acid against strong base

practicals.markdown:
# Potentiometric titration of strong acid against strong base

**Aim:** To determine the normality of the given hydrochloric acid by potentiometric titration with standard sodium hydroxide, locating the end point by the direct, first-derivative and second-derivative methods.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves.

## Principle

A **glass electrode** (indicator electrode, responds to H⁺) and a **saturated calomel** or Ag/AgCl electrode (reference) are dipped in the acid. The cell potential follows the Nernst equation, changing by about 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C; the pH meter shows pH directly.

As NaOH is added, pH rises slowly, then jumps sharply near the equivalence point (about pH 4 to 10 for 0.1 N solutions), then levels off. The end point is:

- the **inflection point** of the pH vs volume curve;
- the **maximum** of ΔpH/ΔV plotted against mean volume (first derivative);
- the volume where **Δ²pH/ΔV²** changes sign, i.e. crosses zero (second derivative).

N(HCl) × V(HCl) = N(NaOH) × V(NaOH at end point)

## Requirements

pH meter with glass and reference electrodes (or a combination electrode), standard buffers (pH 4.0, 7.0, 9.2), standardised 0.1 N NaOH, HCl sample (about 0.1 N), beaker, magnetic stirrer, burette, pipette, graph paper.

## Procedure

1. Calibrate the pH meter with standard buffers at room temperature.
2. Pipette 25 ml of HCl into a beaker; add water if needed to cover the electrode; immerse the electrode and stir gently.
3. Record the initial pH.
4. Add NaOH in 1 ml portions, recording pH after each; near the expected end point (where pH changes quickly) add 0.1–0.2 ml portions.
5. Continue a few ml beyond the end point.
6. Plot (a) pH vs V, (b) ΔpH/ΔV vs mean V, (c) Δ²pH/ΔV² vs V.

## Observations and calculation

| V (ml) | pH | ΔV | ΔpH | ΔpH/ΔV | Mean V | Δ²pH/ΔV² |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 24.6 | 4.0 |  |  |  |  |  |
| 24.8 | 4.3 | 0.2 | 0.3 | 1.5 | 24.7 |  |
| 25.0 | 7.0 | 0.2 | 2.7 | 13.5 | 24.9 | (13.5 − 1.5)/0.2 = +60 |
| 25.2 | 9.7 | 0.2 | 2.7 | 13.5 | 25.1 | (13.5 − 13.5)/0.2 = 0 |
| 25.4 | 10.0 | 0.2 | 0.3 | 1.5 | 25.3 | (1.5 − 13.5)/0.2 = −60 |

The first derivative is highest between 24.9 and 25.1 ml and the second derivative passes through zero at about **25.0 ml**: end point = 25.0 ml.

N(HCl) = 0.1000 × 25.0/25.0 = **0.1000 N** (with a titrant factor, multiply accordingly; for example with 0.0998 N NaOH, N = 0.0998 N).

## Result

The normality of the given hydrochloric acid is ___ N (end point ___ ml).

## Precautions

1. Calibrate the pH meter with buffers at the working temperature.
2. Rinse the electrode between solutions; keep the glass bulb wet and do not wipe it hard.
3. Add small increments near the end point.
4. Stir gently and wait for a stable reading.
5. Do not let the stirrer bar hit the electrode.

## Viva questions

1. **Which electrodes are used?** Glass electrode (indicator) and saturated calomel or Ag/AgCl (reference).
2. **Why is the second derivative most precise?** It locates the exact point where the slope is greatest, as a zero crossing.
3. **What is the pH at the equivalence point here?** About 7 (strong acid–strong base).
4. **Why calibrate with buffers?** To correct for the asymmetry potential and slope of the glass electrode.
5. **Advantages of potentiometric titration?** No indicator; works with coloured or turbid solutions, weak acids and non-aqueous media; can be automated.
practicals.title: Potentiometric titration of strong acid against strong base

questions.answer:
1. Primary standard: substance of high purity whose solution of exactly known strength is made by direct weighing (KHP, anhydrous Na2CO3, K2Cr2O7, KBrO3, NaCl, As2O3).
2. Properties: about 99.9% pure, stable in air (not hygroscopic, not efflorescent, not affected by CO2), unchanged on drying, high equivalent weight, soluble, reacts quickly and stoichiometrically, cheap.
3. Secondary standard: strength found by titration against a primary standard (NaOH, HCl, KMnO4, Na2S2O3, iodine).
4. 0.1 M NaOH: dissolve about 4.2 g NaOH in CO2-free water to 1000 ml (carbonate-free).
5. Standardise: weigh about 0.4 g KHP (Mw 204.22), dissolve in 50 ml water, phenolphthalein, titrate to pink. KHP + NaOH → KNaP + H2O; 1 ml 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 0.02042 g KHP.
6. Example: 0.4085 g KHP needed 19.85 ml; moles = 0.4085/204.22 = 0.002000; M = 0.002000/0.01985 = 0.1008 M (f = 1.008).
7. 0.1 M HCl: about 8.5 ml concentrated HCl diluted to 1000 ml.
8. Standardise against anhydrous Na2CO3 (dried at 270 °C), methyl orange; Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; 1 ml 0.1 M HCl ≡ 0.005299 g Na2CO3.
9. Example: 0.1500 g Na2CO3 needed 28.10 ml; expected = 0.1500/0.005299 = 28.31 ml; f = 28.31/28.10 = 1.007; M = 0.1007.
10. Precautions: triplicate concordant titres (within 0.1 ml), CO2-free water, store NaOH in polythene with soda-lime guard tube.

questions.answer:
1. Error = observed value − true value.
2. Determinate (systematic): definite cause, same direction, correctable — instrumental (uncalibrated burette), reagent (impure reagents), method (incomplete reaction, co-precipitation, indicator error), personal (colour blindness, parallax); constant and proportional errors.
3. Indeterminate (random): small, both directions, no single cause, follow normal distribution; reduced by replicates.
4. Gross errors: blunders such as spillage or wrong reading.
5. Minimising: calibration of apparatus, blank determination, control determination with a standard, independent method, parallel determinations, standard addition, internal standards, pure reagents and good technique.
6. Accuracy = closeness to true value (absolute error, relative error %); precision = closeness of replicates (SD, RSD).
7. Example titres 10.12, 10.15, 10.10, 10.14, 10.14 ml: mean 10.13; deviations −0.01, +0.02, −0.03, +0.01, +0.01; Σd² = 0.0016; s = √(0.0016/4) = 0.02 ml; RSD = 0.20%.
8. If true value 10.00 ml: relative error 1.3% — precise but not accurate, pointing to a systematic error.
9. Significant figures: report burette readings to 0.05 ml, balance to 0.0001 g; round only at the end.

questions.answer:
1. Limit test: semi-quantitative test to show that an impurity is below the permitted limit, by comparing the turbidity/colour/stain of the sample with a standard of the permitted amount under identical conditions; Nessler cylinders used.
2. Chloride: sample + dilute HNO3 + AgNO3 → white AgCl opalescence; compare with standard (known NaCl) after 5 min against black background. HNO3 prevents precipitation of other silver salts (carbonate, phosphate) and gives fine opalescence.
3. Sulphate: sample + dilute HCl + barium sulphate reagent (BaCl2 with alcoholic K2SO4 seed) → BaSO4 turbidity; HCl stops precipitation of BaCO3/phosphate; seed gives uniform turbidity; compare with potassium sulphate standard.
4. Iron: sample + 20% citric acid + thioglycollic acid + ammonia (alkaline) → purple ferrous thioglycollate; citric acid prevents Fe(OH)3 precipitation; thioglycollic acid reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+; compare with ferric ammonium sulphate standard after 5 min.
5. Arsenic (Gutzeit): sample + stannated HCl + KI + SnCl2 + arsenic-free zinc → nascent H reduces arsenic to arsine (AsH3); arsine gives yellow-brown stain on mercuric chloride paper; lead acetate cotton wool absorbs H2S; KI and SnCl2 reduce As(V) to As(III) and give steady evolution; 40 °C for 40 min; compare stain with standard.
6. Result: sample opalescence/colour/stain not more than standard → passes.
7. Diagram of Gutzeit apparatus.
questions.question: What is a limit test? Explain the principle, procedure and reasons for the reagents used in the limit tests for chloride, sulphate, iron and arsenic as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

questions.answer:
1. Accuracy: closeness of a result (or mean) to the true value; expressed as absolute error (X − Xt) or relative error ((X − Xt)/Xt × 100 %, or parts per thousand).
2. Precision: closeness of replicate results to each other; expressed as deviation, average deviation, range, standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)], RSD = s/x̄ × 100.
3. Accuracy is affected by systematic errors; precision by random errors.
4. Results can be precise but inaccurate (tight cluster away from the true value).
5. Good analysis needs both; precision is a necessary but not sufficient condition for accuracy.

questions.answer:
1. Raw materials: impure starting materials (rock salt with Ca/Mg salts; heavy metals in minerals).
2. Reagents in manufacture: residual alkali, ammonia, sulphate.
3. Solvents: tap water ions (Ca, Mg, Cl), residual organic solvents.
4. Reaction vessels: Fe, Cu, Pb from metal plant; alkali from glass.
5. Intermediates and by-products: unreacted p-aminophenol in paracetamol.
6. Manufacturing hazards: dust, fibres, cross-contamination, microbes.
7. Atmosphere: CO2 absorbed by NaOH; moisture.
8. Storage: decomposition by light, air, heat (FeSO4 oxidised to ferric, H2O2 loses oxygen); deliquescence/efflorescence.
9. Containers and closures: leaching of alkali, plasticisers.
10. Deliberate adulteration.
questions.question: Describe the various sources of impurities in pharmaceutical substances with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: arsenic in the sample is reduced by nascent hydrogen (zinc + HCl) to arsine gas, which produces a yellow to brown stain on mercuric chloride paper; the stain is compared with a standard stain.
2. Reagents: stannated HCl, potassium iodide and stannous chloride (reduce As(V) to As(III), steady gas evolution), arsenic-free granulated zinc.
3. Lead acetate cotton wool in the tube absorbs H2S, which would blacken the paper.
4. Apparatus: about 120 ml wide-mouthed bottle, glass tube with lead acetate wool, HgCl2 paper clamped between the flat ends of two tubes.
5. Keep at about 40 °C for 40 minutes; compare stain intensity with the standard prepared from a known arsenic solution under the same conditions.
6. Diagram as in notes.

1. (a) Mw H2SO4 = 98.08; moles = 4.904/98.08 = 0.0500; M = 0.05 M; n = 2 → N = 0.1 N.
2. (b) Mw KMnO4 = 158.03; w = M × Mw × V(L) = 0.02 × 158.03 × 0.5 = 1.580 g. This is 0.1 N (n = 5 in acid).

questions.answer:
1. Dissolve about 25 g Na2S2O3·5H2O (Mw 248.18) and 0.2 g Na2CO3 in freshly boiled and cooled water to 1000 ml; carbonate keeps it slightly alkaline and stable; boiling kills thiosulphate-decomposing bacteria.
2. Standardise with potassium bromate: KBrO3 + 6KI + 6HCl → 3I2 + KBr + 6KCl + 3H2O; liberated iodine titrated with thiosulphate, starch added near the end, blue → colourless.
3. 1 ml 0.1 M Na2S2O3 ≡ 0.002784 g KBrO3 (167.00/6/10).
4. Alternative: K2Cr2O7 + KI + HCl, 1 ml ≡ 0.004903 g K2Cr2O7.
5. Example: 0.1225 g K2Cr2O7 used 24.80 ml; expected 24.98 ml; f = 1.007; M = 0.1007.
6. Precautions: stoppered flask, keep in dark, add starch late, do not titrate in strong acid.
questions.question: Describe the preparation and standardisation of 0.1 M sodium thiosulphate.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: iron reacts with thioglycollic acid in alkaline (ammoniacal) solution containing citric acid to form a purple ferrous thioglycollate complex; colour compared with a standard iron solution.
2. Procedure: dissolve sample in water in a Nessler cylinder, add 2 ml of 20% w/v iron-free citric acid and 0.1 ml thioglycollic acid, make alkaline with iron-free ammonia, dilute to 50 ml, stand 5 min; compare with standard from ferric ammonium sulphate.
3. Citric acid forms a soluble complex with iron and prevents precipitation of iron hydroxide when ammonia is added.
4. Thioglycollic acid reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+ so all iron is measured, and forms the coloured complex.
5. Sample colour less than standard → passes.
questions.question: Explain the limit test for iron. Why are citric acid and thioglycollic acid used?

questions.answer: A substance of very high purity and stability whose solution of exactly known concentration can be made by direct weighing. Examples: potassium hydrogen phthalate, anhydrous sodium carbonate (also K2Cr2O7, NaCl).
questions.question: Define a primary standard and give two examples.

questions.answer: An official book of drug standards (identity, purity, assay, storage) published under government authority and legally binding. The Indian Pharmacopoeia is published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.
